title: Tertiary education
description: Third stage of education for adults
wiki_lead:
Tertiary education is a stage of education following compulsory education. Depending on the definition used it may include all post-compulsory education, including that delivered at secondary schools, all post-secondary education, or be a synonym for higher education. Historically, it has covered education between the end of compulsory schooling and the start of higher education (then referred to as post-tertiary education). Tertiary education may be defined by life-stage as including adult education at all educational levels, including basic skills education, or may be defined by educational level as only including education at the higher education level.
Tertiary education may culminate in the receipt of certificates, diplomas, or academic degrees, or may be lifelong learning that does not result in formal certification. Higher education is taken to include undergraduate and postgraduate education, representing levels 5, 6, 7, and 8 of the 2011 version of the International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED) structure, while vocational education beyond secondary education is known as further education in the United Kingdom, or included under the category of continuing education in the United States.
UNESCO has stated that tertiary education focuses on learning endeavours in specialised fields. It includes academic and higher vocational education. The World Bank's 2019 World Development Report on the future of work argues that, given the future of work and the increasing role of technology in value chains, tertiary education is becoming even more relevant for workers to compete in the labor market.

UNESCO has stated that tertiary education focuses on learning endeavours in specialised fields. It includes academic and higher vocational education. The World Bank's 2019 World Development Report on the future of work argues that, given the future of work and the increasing role of technology in value chains, tertiary education is becoming even more relevant for workers to compete in the labor market.


Definitions
Tertiary education has a number of definitions. It may include all post-compulsory education, including that delivered at secondary schools, all post-secondary education, or be a synonym for higher education. Historically, it has covered education between the end of compulsory schooling and the start of higher education (then referred to as post-tertiary education), but is normally now taken to also include higher education. Tertiary education may be defined by life-stage as including adult education at all educational levels, including basic skills education, or may be defined by educational level as only including education at the higher education level.
While tertiary education is sometimes used as a synonym for higher education, the two terms are distinct. In an international context, tertiary education takes in technical and vocational education and training as well as higher education. Various other definitions are used in specific countries.
In the ISCED, tertiary education is used as an educational level, rather than an educational stage, to refer to education at ISCED levels 5, 6, 7 and 8. This takes in academic education as well as degree-level technical and professional education. This is synonymous with the definition for higher education as "Education at ISCED level 5 or above".


Components
There are multiple, overlapping components to tertiary education, not all of which are included in all definitions of tertiary education.


Higher education

Higher education covers tertiary education at degree level.


Technical and vocational education and training

Technical and vocational education and training (TVET), also known as vocational education and training, technical and vocational skills development, further education and training, and technical and further education, includes formal education at colleges, apprenticeships, and lifelong learning. The defining feature is the orientation towards employment, and the educational may be at secondary, post-secondary or degree-level.


Adult education

Tertiary education can include post-compulsory lifelong learning or adult education at all educational levels, sometimes known as continuing education, recurrent education, or second chance education.

grok_lead: Tertiary education refers to all formal post-secondary education, including programs at public and private universities, colleges, technical training institutes, and community colleges, which build on secondary education to provide advanced learning activities in specialized fields. It typically requires successful completion of secondary schooling for admission and leads to qualifications ranging from certificates to advanced research degrees. Globally, participation in tertiary education has expanded markedly, with the gross enrolment ratioâthe number of students enrolled regardless of age relative to the typical age groupâreaching over 40% in many OECD countries by the early 2020s. Across OECD nations, the share of 25- to 64-year-olds holding a postsecondary degree rose from 32% in 2012 to 41% in 2022, reflecting policy efforts to boost human capital amid economic demands for skilled labor. This growth has been driven by both public investments and private demand, particularly in fields like science, technology, engineering, and mathematics, which correlate with higher economic returns. Empirical studies consistently demonstrate that higher levels of tertiary education attainment contribute to economic growth, with expansions in educated workforces associated with increased GDP per capita and regional productivity. For instance, a 10% increase in universities per capita within a region links to 0.4% higher future GDP per capita, underscoring the role of institutions in fostering innovation and knowledge spillovers. However, these benefits vary by field, with STEM disciplines showing stronger growth impacts than humanities or social sciences. Despite these advantages, tertiary education faces scrutiny over its quality, accessibility, and value amid rising costs and uneven outcomes. In the United States, for example, low on-time completion rates and substantial student debt have fueled debates on whether mass expansion has diluted returns, with many graduates facing underemployment. Additionally, empirical evidence reveals pronounced ideological homogeneity among faculty, with over 60% identifying as liberal or far-left in recent surveys, contributing to self-censorship among students and potential suppression of viewpoint diversity. This skew, more evident in social sciences and humanities than in hard sciences, raises concerns about institutional bias influencing research and pedagogy, though direct causal effects on student learning remain debated.
